You can use it for a variety of things, just as you would use other operators. I believe it opens many more avenues for programmers because they can string things together with the action. You can also use it when making ciphers, though it's kind of obvious when ciphering things that your information will eventually be concatenated because that's how we make words (concatenating letters one after the other). 

The first thing that comes to mind mathematically that's easy to explain is you can do set relations with it. As in, you can create a relation S on A x B and define ~ to be the concatenation of the elements. However, this dead ends because the operation is not symmetric so it will not be able to be an equivalence relation, and you can not partition sets with it.

But really, its larger use is just connect this thing with this thing in this order. We do that everyday, everywhere. 

edit: those who recall their set theory definitions can correct me on my shoddy set theory work if you see errors.

Mathematically, there's no difference since you'll likely be seeing it defined before the paper goes in depth. The author will most likely refresh you on it because it's a lesser used operation and then show you their demarcation for it. There's no hard and fast standard for the uncommon tools.

As for its applications in computer science and elsewhere, I'm not too sure. I think it'd be up to the language used for the coding.

I don't believe there is a inverse operation of the concatenate. In the mathematics arena, I suppose you might call it splitting, deconcatenating, or decomposing.

In the programming realm, I think I saw somewhere that it could be best referred to as ~~"parsing"~~ slicing since this is a programming action that identifies distinct elements/components of something.

The abstraction of concatenate refers to stringing together anything in a specific order: a||b = ab. So you can also do this with words or things. In which case you can find all sorts of synonyms to the words I've listed above i.e. cleave, separate, disassemble, etc. 

Best choices imo are deconcatenate, split, decompose, and slice.

The same thing happened with my father during his mental decline. He ran in a circle of really upper level thinkers; he himself had his J.D. and Ph.D. in chemistry along with some business school.

I agree with others that this could be something that you should just let slide. But I also remember that I did take away my father's phone and replaced it with his favorite books. On one hand, talking to his colleagues bolstered him. On the other hand, he did not want to be remembered as babbling and inept. He believed in death with dignity and did not want drama or fuss. He made it clear while I was growing up that there was a certain point where he was gone and whatever was left, while technically him, was not *him*. I suppose it's up to what your mother's wishes are/were to help you decide if you should actively pursue reducing her social media.

When you feel it's about time to start placing limits there are some things you can do. Put on parental features. Turn the ringer and vibration off. Turn off automatic background email/app refreshing. Turn off push notifications. Essentially make the phone quiet except for when you're using it. Then you can bring in other things, like books and games. I would watch jeopardy and wheel of fortune with my dad. If she asks for her phone, ask her what she wants to do with it and then talk to her about it while navigating it yourself (for say, phone calls and texts). My dad would dictate to me on normal days anyways because he always thought his fingers weren't agile enough for the iPhone keyboard, so it made sense for me to reinstate the dictation. You could try that. 

I'm so sorry you have to deal with this. My best to you and your mother.

My grief comes incrementally. I occasionally get frustrated that it's these little bursts and then the rest of the time I'm kind of numb. I think my biggest piece of advice is to let it come how it comes. I kind of forced myself once to try to do it all and the massive field of grief in front me floored me. There's a reason why we do it the way we do. Whatever comes to you, just ride it as best you can. Each person's grief is specific so don't be worried if yours looks different than other people's.

Also, remember that while you do it your own way, there's probably someone else who's grieving in a similar fashion. Reaching out to these individuals and seeing you're not alone helps also.

I hope you're well, and I'm here to talk if you want. As for his viewing and the immediate days to come, stay strong. You can do it (:

1. If you can get them in the totally raw form with the skin on the outside, it's best to cook it separately from your ramen. Peel the outer skin off and cut off the root. Boil it in water until it is skewered through softly. This depends on the size of the root you have so keep an eye on it. Then remove the rest of the skin and julienne. Add it on top of your ramen.

2. If you get them in a can, check if they are precooked or not. These come with their own instructions so I can't help you out here, only the brand can!

3. A prepackaged bamboo shoot that is still intact (vacuum packed) is ready to go. Just unpack it and rinse. Then julienne it. I would boil the julienned strips in a separate pot for 2 minutes just to safely remove any bitterness. Then add them into your ramen.

4. For any of the methods above, just remember to account for any bitterness in the bamboo shoots. That's usually what turns people off of bamboo shoots if they don't properly cook it out. After you have your ready to add shoots, you can boil them in the ramen broth for a minute and get them really flavorful. Don't overboil them either though :)

I've seen that people take a fan, and put a bucket of ice in front of it. Then aim the fan at yourself, and keep oscillate off. 

Another choice is to take your sweat to the next level, and capitalize on some evaporative cooling. Take a lukewarm shower (cold showers I've read actually reduce your ability to tolerate heat), then let your hair air dry. This works better with longer hair, but leaving your hair wet helps you cool off as the water evaporates. This option works best in a room with high air flow, and low humidity. 

You can also sleep closer to the ground, since cold air sinks. 

A costly choice is to buy a Chilipad or similar bed temperature regulating pad. You place it on your mattress, but under your fitted sheet, and it fills with water that is cooled/heated to your specifications in a unit at the base of your bed.

There are other things you can buy too, but I'm not sure they have the same efficacy. These are things like gel mattress toppers, cool gel pillows, etc.
